1	1
Grammar Summary Part 1
Bac
Nouns
Nouns are words that represent people, places, things, animals, ideas, & feelings.
E.g., invention/ technology/ brain/ agency, satisfaction, etc.
How to get plural nouns?
Most of the time, you simply need to add an “s” to the end of the noun, as in “chairs.” However, other
nouns require other methods:
• If the noun ends in -s, -x, -ch, -o, or -sh, add es to the end of the word.
 E.g., potatoes/ boxes/ matches
• If the noun ends in a consonant and a -y, replace the -y with an i and add es.
 E.g., family → families / baby→ babies / country→ countries
• If the noun ends in -is, replace the -is with “es”.
 E.g., crisis → crises/ analysis → analyses
• If the noun ends in -f, replace the -f with v and add “es”.
 E.g., loaf→ loaves/ leaf→ leaves/ wolf → wolves
• If the noun ends in -fe, replace the -f with “v” and add “s”.
 E.g., wife → wives / life→ lives / knife → knives
• If the noun ends in -us, replace the -us with “i”.
 E.g., stimulus→ stimuli /focus → foci
• If the noun contains -oo, replace the -oo with “ee”.
 E.g., tooth → teeth/ foot → feet
• If the noun ends in -on, replace the -on with “a”.
 E.g., criterion → criteria/ phenomenon → phenomena

However, some nouns do not change (e.g., “sheep” and “series”), and some do not follow the rules
above. For example, “moose” does not become “meese” and “café” does not become “caves.”
➔ Learning to spot these special cases takes time and practice.
Pronouns
Pronouns are words that replace nouns in sentences to make our speech less repetitive.
To use a pronoun, you must make sure you have already identified the noun it will replace in the sentence.

❖ My father is a hard-working man. He works so hard to make ends meet. I appreciate him very
much.
❖ The Stewarts live here. Why don’t we stop by and visit (they) them?
❖ Relax, Carla. The children are old enough to look after (they) themselves.
❖ That money is neither (me) mine nor (she) hers.
❖ Don’t play with that knife! You might hurt (you) yourself.
❖ Which one is yours? The white or the gray?
❖ Can you see the guys over there? Those are the new exchange students. Would you like to go
and say hi to them?
Who Whom
✓ Refers to the subject of a sentence.
Who baked the cake?
Jane did.
She did.
✓ Refers to the object of a verb or preposition.
Whom will you vote for?
I will vote for Carlos.
I will vote for him.
➢ Who decorated the house? → Jane (she) decorated the house.
➢ Whom did you invite to the party? I invited Beth (her).
➢ Whom did she meet at the restaurant? She met Willy (him).
➢ With whom will you have dinner? I will have dinner with Leo (him).
➢ You won’t believe who drove me home! → Jacob (he) drove me home.

Adverbs
Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Examples: ‘quickly’, ‘very’ and ‘soon’.
E.g.:
She hurriedly answered the door.
I am terribly sick of your lies!
Mothers are almost always right.
➔ We usually get an adverb by adding ‘ly’ to the adjective form of the word.
Quiet → quietly
Painful → painfully
Nice → nicely
Adjectives ending in ‘able’ or ‘ible’ → remove the ‘e’ + y
Regrettable → regrettably
Horrible → horribly
Terrible → terribly
Adjectives ending in ‘ue’ → remove the ‘e’ + “-ly”
True → truly
Due → Duly
Adjectives ending in ‘y’ → remove the ‘y’ + ily
Happy → happily
Easy → easily
Ready → readily
Exception to this is when the y has the /ɑı/ sound, not the /Iː/ sound: shy ⇒ shyly, sly ⇒ slyly
Adjectives ending in ‘ic’ → + ally
Scientific → scientifically
Historic → historically
Economic → economically

Consider the following words? Are they adverbs?
Friendly/ lovely/ lonely/ lively/ costly/ silly/ bubbly/ curly/ deadly/ ugly/ smelly/ oily/ timely…
➔ They are adjectives!
There are adverbs that do not follow any of the rules above; they are called irregular adverbs.
Adjective Adverb
Good Well
Late Late
Fast Fast
Far Far
Hard Hard
Early Early
Daily Daily
Weekly Weekly
Straight Straight/ straightly
Wrong Wrong/ wrongly
➢ He is a hard-working man. (adjective)
➢ He works hard. (adverb)
➢ She is a fast driver. (adjective)

6	6
Grammar Summary Part 1

➢ She drives fast. (adverb)
➢ We drove as fast as we could, but we were late. (adjective)
➢ We drove as fast as we could, but we arrived late. (adverb)
Note that ‘lately’ means ‘recently’ and ‘hardly’ is used to mean ‘unkindly’ or ‘harshly’ – (e.g.,
He treated her hardly), but more usually it means mean ‘very scarce’ – (e.g., There is hardly any
bread left) or ‘almost not’ – (e.g., I can hardly see the sign.)
It is important to remember that linking verbs (such as be, become, get, and the sense verbs
feel, taste, look, sound, smell, and seem) are followed by predicative adjectives, not adverbs. For
example:
You seem exhausted.
She sounds American. (An opinion based on her voice.)
We became famous.
You look good.
You look well. =/= you look sick.
Notice that the last two examples are both correct. Not only is well an adverb, but it also functions
as an adjective. Its opposite adjective is ill, while the opposite of good is bad. When we say, “You look
good,” we are referring to the person’s physical appearance. If, on the other hand, we say, “You look
well,” we are referring to the health or well-being of the person.

Compound Adjectives
 A compound adjective is formed when two or more words are combined together to modify the
same noun.
 They are usually hyphenated.
Type Example
Noun-ing verb It’s a record-breaking performance.
Noun-past participle We need to create more wind-powered products.
Noun-adjective It’s a snow-white dress.
Noun-like I like reading novels about life-like events.
Number-singular noun-old He is a 99-year-old man.
Number-singular noun It’s a five-minute walk.
Number-noun + ed It’s a three-eyed creature.
Ordinal number-noun Buying second-hand clothes is an effective measure to protect the
environment.
Adjective-adjective It’s a dark-green leaflet.
Adjective-noun Bill has a full-time job.
Adjective-noun + ed Mandy is a strong-willed girl.
Adjective-past participle The U.S. takes advantage of its brainy foreign-born immigrants.
Adjective-ing verb Henry is a hard-working guy.
Adverb-ing verb It’s a forward-thinking plan.
Adverb-past participle Mike is a well-raised kid.

-- 7 of 15 --

© TakiAcademy.com
8	8
Grammar Summary Part 1
Bac
Remarks
 A compound modifier only needs a hyphen when it comes before a noun. If it comes after the noun,
leave the hyphen out.
➔ She works full time. Vs. She is a full-time worker.
➔ The hotel is well known. Vs. It is a well-known hotel.
 Do not use a hyphen when you have a compound modifier that consists of an adverb ending in -ly plus
a participle or adjective.
➔ He is a highly respected man.
➔ She was utterly shocked.
➔ This is an extremely dangerous step.
 When you have a compound modifier that is interrupted by some other word that’s not really part of
the modifier, use a suspended hyphen.
➔ It is a five- or ten-minute walk.
➔ He is a seventeen- or eighteen-year-old boy.

The Comparative Form
What are long adjectives?
2-syllable adjectives not ending in “y” (pleasant/ peaceful/ thoughtful/ careful).
3-syllable adjectives or more (necessary/ beautiful/ dangerous/ delicious/ positive/ comfortable/
glorious).
What are short adjectives?
1-syllable adjectives (tall/ old/ long/ short/ wise/ large/ big/ huge/ thin/ fat).
2-syllable adjectives ending in “y” (happy/ angry/ hungry/ busy/ windy).
2-syllable adjectives ending in er/ le/ ow (queer/clever/ eager/ tender/ gentle/ simple/ narrow/ shallow).
What are irregular adjectives?
They are adjectives that do not abide by the rules.
Long adjectives Short adjectives Irregular adjectives

more expensive than

➔ Caracas is (expensive) less
expensive than Singapore.

trains.

→ bigger/ thinner/ fatter

Nouns
Nouns are words that represent people, places, things, animals, ideas, & feelings.
E.g., invention/ technology/ brain/ agency, satisfaction, etc.
How to get plural nouns?
Most of the time, you simply need to add an “s” to the end of the noun, as in “chairs.” However, other
nouns require other methods:
• If the noun ends in -s, -x, -ch, -o, or -sh, add es to the end of the word.
 E.g., potatoes/ boxes/ matches
• If the noun ends in a consonant and a -y, replace the -y with an i and add es.
 E.g., family → families / baby→ babies / country→ countries
• If the noun ends in -is, replace the -is with “es”.
 E.g., crisis → crises/ analysis → analyses
• If the noun ends in -f, replace the -f with v and add “es”.
 E.g., loaf→ loaves/ leaf→ leaves/ wolf → wolves
• If the noun ends in -fe, replace the -f with “v” and add “s”.
 E.g., wife → wives / life→ lives / knife → knives
• If the noun ends in -us, replace the -us with “i”.
 E.g., stimulus→ stimuli /focus → foci
• If the noun contains -oo, replace the -oo with “ee”.
 E.g., tooth → teeth/ foot → feet
• If the noun ends in -on, replace the -on with “a”.
 E.g., criterion → criteria/ phenomenon → phenomena

Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Examples: ‘quickly’, ‘very’ and ‘soon’.

➢ She drives fast. (adverb)
➢ We drove as fast as we could, but we were late. (adjective)
➢ We drove as fast as we could, but we arrived late. (adverb)
Note that ‘lately’ means ‘recently’ and ‘hardly’ is used to mean ‘unkindly’ or ‘harshly’ – (e.g.,
He treated her hardly), but more usually it means mean ‘very scarce’ – (e.g., There is hardly any
bread left) or ‘almost not’ – (e.g., I can hardly see the sign.)
It is important to remember that linking verbs (such as be, become, get, and the sense verbs
feel, taste, look, sound, smell, and seem) are followed by predicative adjectives, not adverbs. For
example:
You seem exhausted.
She sounds American. (An opinion based on her voice.)
We became famous.
You look good.
You look well. =/= you look sick.
Notice that the last two examples are both correct. Not only is well an adverb, but it also functions
as an adjective. Its opposite adjective is ill, while the opposite of good is bad. When we say, “You look
good,” we are referring to the person’s physical appearance. If, on the other hand, we say, “You look
well,” we are referring to the health or well-being of the person.
